script.title: The math of freelance pricing: billable hours, discounts and raises
script.hook: If you've ever quoted a price and then lain awake wondering if it was too high, or too low, this video is for you. Pricing feels like a guess, but most of it is arithmetic. In the next few minutes we'll build an hourly rate from the life you want to pay for, turn it into a day rate and a project price, and then do the math on the three decisions that cost freelancers the most money: how many hours you plan to bill, whether to give a discount, and when to raise your rate. Every number is on screen. Education, not tax advice, using twenty twenty-six federal figures.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you've ever quoted a price and then lain awake wondering if it was too high, or too low, this video is for you. Pricing feels like a guess, but most of it is arithmetic. In the next few minutes we'll build an hourly rate from the life you want to pay for, turn it into a day rate and a project price, and then do the math on the three decisions that cost freelancers the most money: how many hours you plan to bill, whether to give a discount, and when to raise your rate. Every number is on screen. Education, not tax advice, using twenty twenty-six federal figures.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes at a whiteboard with simple sums. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The target
segments.narration: We start with what you want to take home, not with what other people charge. Our example freelancer, Alex, is fictional. Alex wants fifty-five thousand dollars a year to live on. As an employee, someone else paid for health insurance and matched retirement savings. Now Alex pays for both: six thousand dollars of health insurance and five thousand into retirement. So Alex needs sixty-six thousand dollars a year after tax. That number, not a salary, is the starting point.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three coin stacks adding up. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Tax
segments.narration: Next, tax. Alex pays self-employment tax, which is fifteen point three percent on ninety-two point three five percent of profit, and then income tax on top. To keep sixty-six thousand, Alex needs about eighty-four thousand dollars of profit. Federal tax on eighty-four thousand, for a single filer with no other income, is about seventeen thousand six hundred. If Alex's state has income tax, the profit needed goes up again. This is the step people skip when they compare their rate with their old salary.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall coin stack with a slice taken off. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Revenue
segments.narration: Profit is what's left after business costs. Alex spends about six thousand dollars a year on software, a laptop, insurance and fees. So the revenue Alex needs is eighty-four thousand plus six thousand: ninety thousand dollars. This is the number every pricing decision has to add up to. Write yours down. If you're not sure of your costs, look at last year's Schedule C, line twenty-eight, total expenses.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a small block on top. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hours
segments.narration: Now the most important assumption: billable hours. A full-time job is two thousand and eighty hours a year. A freelancer doesn't bill anything close to that. Finding clients, writing proposals, invoicing, email, bookkeeping and learning all take time nobody pays for. Alex plans on twenty-five billable hours a week for forty-eight weeks, leaving four weeks for holidays, vacation and sick days. That's twelve hundred billable hours. Ninety thousand divided by twelve hundred is seventy-five dollars an hour. That's Alex's floor.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with shaded blocks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hours chart
segments.narration: Let's put that on a chart, because this is where most rates go wrong. Same target, same costs, only the billable hours change. At thirty-five hours a week, Alex needs about fifty-four dollars an hour. At thirty, sixty-two fifty. At twenty-five, seventy-five. At twenty, about ninety-four. If you set your rate assuming thirty-five billable hours and you're actually billing twenty-two, you're not lazy and you're not failing. Your rate was built on the wrong number. Most freelancers find their real number is between twenty and thirty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bar chart with four bars. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: Hourly floor for $90,000
chart.note: 48 working weeks. Same target and costs; only billable hours change.

segments.heading: Day rate
segments.narration: Some clients prefer a day rate. The temptation is to multiply your hourly rate by eight. But a day of client work still has email, calls, travel and context switching around it. Six billable hours is more realistic. Seventy-five times six is four hundred fifty dollars a day. Sanity check: four days a week, for forty-eight weeks, is about eighty-six thousand four hundred dollars. Close to the target, which is the point. A day rate is the same target, packaged differently.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a sun-shaped clock with six segments. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Project price
segments.narration: For projects, estimate the hours honestly, multiply by your floor, then add a buffer for revisions and surprises. Twenty percent is a common buffer. Say a website will take forty hours. Forty times seventy-five is three thousand. Plus twenty percent is three thousand six hundred. The client sees a project price, not an hourly rate, so they compare outcomes rather than hours. And if you get faster over time, your effective hourly rate goes up instead of your income going down.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a project folder with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Discounts
segments.narration: Now the first costly decision: discounts. A twenty percent discount sounds like it costs twenty percent. It costs more. On a ten-thousand-dollar project, twenty percent off is eight thousand. To get back to ten thousand of revenue, you need two thousand more of work, and two thousand is twenty-five percent of eight thousand. At thirty percent off, you need forty-three percent more work. At half price, you need to double your work just to stand still.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two bars, one stretched. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Scope trades
segments.narration: So when a client says the price is too high, trade scope instead of rate. Offer fewer deliverables, fewer rounds of revisions, a longer timeline you can fit around other work, or have the client do part of it, like gathering content. The sentence is simple: I can do it for eight thousand if we drop this part. The client gets a lower price, you keep your rate, and the next project starts from the right number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. scissors cutting a list. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Raises
segments.narration: The second decision is raising your rate, and it's usually the one with the best return. Alex bills twelve hundred hours at seventy-five: ninety thousand. Suppose Alex raises to eighty-five, about thirteen percent, and loses ten percent of the hours because a client or two leaves. Ten eighty hours at eighty-five is ninety-one thousand eight hundred. That's more revenue, and a hundred and twenty hours back. Three working weeks.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a slightly taller coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Break-even
segments.narration: Here's how to find your own break-even. Divide this year's revenue by the new rate. Ninety thousand divided by eighty-five is about ten fifty-nine hours. That's the fewest hours Alex can bill at the new rate and still match this year. Twelve hundred minus ten fifty-nine is about a hundred and forty hours, so Alex could lose about one billable hour in eight before being worse off. Most rate increases don't lose anything like that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale level. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Notice
segments.narration: How to raise it: give existing clients thirty to sixty days' notice, keep work that's already booked at the old rate, and keep the message short. Something like: starting the first of next quarter, my rate for new work will be eighty-five dollars an hour; anything already scheduled stays at the current rate. Don't apologize and don't list your costs. New clients simply get the new rate from day one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an envelope with a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Market check
segments.narration: Your floor is the least you can charge. It's not necessarily the right price. Compare it with what experienced people in your niche charge, which you can find in industry surveys, job boards and by asking peers. If the market pays more than your floor, charge more. If the market pays less than your floor, the fix is usually a narrower niche, a stronger offer or packaged projects, not a lower rate you can't live on.
segments.on_screen_text: Floor vs market: take the higher
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two bars, one marked floor. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Concentration
segments.narration: One more number that belongs in pricing: how much of your revenue comes from one client. If Alex's biggest client is sixty percent of the ninety thousand, losing them leaves thirty-six thousand. That's a crisis. At thirty percent, losing them leaves sixty-three thousand. That's a hard quarter. A big client can also push your rate down, because you can't afford to lose them. Keeping any one client under about a third gives you room to price properly.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with one large slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Four pricing mistakes to avoid. One: dividing by two thousand and eighty hours. Two: forgetting that you pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare. Three: giving a percentage discount instead of trading scope. Four: never raising your rate, so inflation cuts your pay every year without you noticing. Fix those four, and most freelancers find their rate was too low, not too high.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Start from take-home plus health and retirement. Gross it up for tax to find the profit you need. Add business costs to get revenue. Divide by honest billable hours to get your floor. Multiply by six for a day rate, and by estimated hours plus a buffer for projects. Trade scope instead of discounting. Raise your rate with notice, and check your break-even. The free rate calculator in the description does the tax part for you. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

segments.heading: Tax home
segments.narration: It starts with your tax home. For a freelancer, that's generally the city or area where your business is based, which for most people is where you live and work. Travel expenses are deductible when you're away from your tax home overnight, or long enough that you need sleep or rest, for business. A day trip to a client across town isn't travel; it's local transportation, which follows the mileage rules instead. Travel means you're sleeping somewhere else because of work.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a house with a moon above it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Primarily business
segments.narration: Next comes the key question: is the trip primarily for business? For travel inside the United States, you look at the days. If you spend more days on business than on personal activities, the trip is primarily business. Business days include days you travel to and from the business location, and days you spend at meetings, conferences or client work. Keep a simple list of each day and what it was for. That list is what makes everything else deductible.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a scale tipped toward a briefcase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Transportation
segments.narration: If the trip is primarily business, your transportation there and back is deductible in full. That includes flights, train tickets, or driving your own car at the standard mileage rate. It also includes baggage fees, and getting between the airport and your hotel, and between your hotel and the client or conference venue. If the trip is primarily personal, the transportation isn't deductible at all, even if you do some work while you're there.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a plane, a train and a car. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lodging
segments.narration: Lodging is deductible for the nights you need to be there for business. If you stay longer for personal reasons, those extra nights are yours to pay. Lodging should be reasonable, not lavish, but there's no fixed limit; a normal business hotel in that city is fine. Keep the folio, the itemized bill, not just the card statement, because it shows the nightly rate and any extras.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a hotel with some windows lit. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Meals
segments.narration: Meals while you're traveling for business are generally fifty percent deductible. That covers your own meals on business days, not just meals with clients. The usual rules apply: not lavish, and you need a record of the amount, date, place and business reason. Room service, a sandwich at the airport, dinner near the conference: all count at half. Alcohol bought with a meal is part of the meal.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a plate with half shaded. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Per diem
segments.narration: There's a shortcut for meals. As a self-employed person, instead of keeping every meal receipt, you can use the federal per diem rate for meals and incidental expenses for the city you're in. You look it up on the GSA per diem site by city and month, and multiply the daily rate by your business days, with seventy-five percent on travel days. The fifty percent limit still applies to the total. The shortcut is for meals only. Lodging always has to be your actual cost, with receipts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop showing a rate table. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Let's put it together. Jamie, a fictional consultant, flies to a client workshop: four business days, then two days at the beach. Flight: four hundred dollars, fully deductible, because four business days beat two personal ones. Hotel: six nights at a hundred and eighty, but only four nights were needed for business: seven hundred and twenty. Meals on business days: two hundred forty dollars, at fifty percent is a hundred and twenty. Total deduction: twelve hundred and forty dollars.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three coins adding to a stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Personal days
segments.narration: Now flip it. If Jamie had two business days and four beach days, the trip would be primarily personal. The flight wouldn't be deductible at all. Jamie could still deduct the lodging and meals for the two business days, and the conference fee itself, but not the cost of getting there. That's why the day count matters so much, and why it's worth writing down before you book, not reconstructing it afterwards.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a plane crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Weekends
segments.narration: What about a weekend in the middle? If you have business on Friday and again on Monday, the weekend days in between can count as business days when staying is reasonable, for example because flying home and back would cost more. The days themselves count, and so do the lodging and meals for them. A weekend after the work is finished, though, is personal.
segments.on_screen_text: A weekend between business days can count
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a bridged weekend. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Conferences
segments.narration: Conference fees are deductible when the conference relates to your current business, the same test as for courses. A design conference for a designer: yes. A cooking retreat for a designer: no. Keep the agenda, because the IRS can ask what the event covered. Workshops, trade shows and industry meetups all count the same way. Membership fees for professional associations are generally deductible too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a lanyard badge. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Family along
segments.narration: Bringing your partner or kids? Their travel costs are personal, unless they work for your business and have a real business reason to be there. You can still deduct your own share. For the hotel, that's what a single room would have cost, which is often the same as the room you shared. For the car, the mileage is the same however many people are inside. Meals for family members aren't deductible.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a car with several passengers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Foreign trips
segments.narration: Travel outside the US has extra rules. If a trip abroad lasts more than a week and a quarter or more of it is personal, you generally split even the airfare between business and personal days. Conventions outside North America have their own limits too. For a foreign trip, read the travel chapter of Publication four sixty-three before you book.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a globe with a small warning sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Records make all of this work. For each trip, keep: the dates you left and came back, a list of business days and what you did, receipts for lodging and anything over seventy-five dollars, and a note of the business purpose. A calendar entry plus a folder of receipts is enough. A photo of each receipt, saved the day you get it, beats a pocket of crumpled paper in October.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder with a calendar on top. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Four travel mistakes. One: deducting a mostly personal trip because you answered a few emails. Two: deducting every night when only some were for business. Three: deducting meals at a hundred percent. Four: using per diem for lodging, which isn't allowed for the self-employed. Avoid those, and travel is one of the more valuable deductions a freelancer has.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Driving
segments.narration: Driving instead of flying? For a road trip that's primarily business, you can deduct your car costs at the standard mileage rate, seventy-two and a half cents a mile for twenty twenty-six, plus parking and tolls. Log the odometer at the start and the end, and note any personal side trips, which you subtract. If you rent a car for the trip, the rental is a travel expense instead, along with fuel. Either way, mileage from your hotel to the client's office each day counts too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a car on a winding road. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where it goes
segments.narration: On your return, travel goes on Schedule C. Flights, hotels, rental cars and taxis go on line twenty-four a, travel. Meals go on line twenty-four b, at the deductible fifty percent. Car mileage goes on line nine, car and truck expenses. Conference fees usually go under other expenses or education. Keeping those categories separate in your bookkeeping as you go makes filing quick.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with highlighted lines. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Travel counts when you're away from your tax home overnight for business. If business days outnumber personal days, transportation is fully deductible. Lodging counts for business nights, and meals at fifty percent, or use the per diem rate for meals only. Weekends between business days can count. Deduct only your share when family comes. Keep a day list and receipts. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: Hiring help as a freelancer: contractors, family and the forms you need
script.hook: Getting too busy to do everything yourself? At some point most freelancers pay someone else: a subcontractor to take overflow work, a virtual assistant, a bookkeeper, or maybe a teenager at home who can pack orders over the summer. Each of those comes with different tax rules, and getting the label wrong can be expensive. In this video: how to tell a contractor from an employee, what to collect before you pay anyone, which forms you owe in January, and the special rules for paying your own family. Education, not tax or legal advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Getting too busy to do everything yourself? At some point most freelancers pay someone else: a subcontractor to take overflow work, a virtual assistant, a bookkeeper, or maybe a teenager at home who can pack orders over the summer. Each of those comes with different tax rules, and getting the label wrong can be expensive. In this video: how to tell a contractor from an employee, what to collect before you pay anyone, which forms you owe in January, and the special rules for paying your own family. Education, not tax or legal advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a smaller helper at a desk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Contractor or employee
segments.narration: The first question is whether the person is an independent contractor or an employee. You don't get to choose the label; the facts decide it. The IRS looks at the whole relationship and groups the evidence into three areas: behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship. No single factor decides it. It's the overall picture of who controls the work.
segments.on_screen_text: The facts decide, not the label
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a magnifying glass over two name tags. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Behavioral
segments.narration: Behavioral control is about how the work gets done. If you tell the person when and where to work, what tools to use, what order to do things in, and you train them in your way of doing it, that points toward employee. If you describe the result you want and they decide how to get there, on their own schedule, that points toward contractor. A copywriter who delivers drafts by a deadline looks like a contractor. An assistant who works your hours on your system looks more like an employee.
segments.on_screen_text: Who controls how the work is done?
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a hand holding puppet strings, crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Financial
segments.narration: Financial control looks at the money side. Contractors usually invest in their own equipment, have other clients, can make or lose money on a job, set their own prices, and send you invoices. Employees are usually paid by the hour or by salary, use your equipment, and can't really make a loss. If the person markets their services to the public and has a business of their own, that's strong evidence of a contractor.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a toolbox and an invoice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Relationship
segments.narration: The type of relationship covers the rest: whether there's a written contract, whether you provide benefits like paid time off, whether the work is expected to go on indefinitely, and whether it's a key part of your regular business. A written contract helps, but it doesn't override the facts. If you pay someone indefinitely, set their hours and give them paid vacation, calling them a contractor doesn't make them one.
segments.on_screen_text: Contract, benefits, how long it lasts
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a contract next to a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wrong label
segments.narration: Why it matters: if the IRS decides someone you treated as a contractor was really an employee, you can owe the payroll taxes you didn't withhold or pay, plus penalties and interest. States have their own tests too, and some are stricter than the federal one. If you're unsure, you can ask the IRS for a determination on Form S S eight, though it takes time. For most freelancers, the simple answer is to hire contractors who really do run their own business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a stack of forms with a red stamp. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Before paying
segments.narration: Before you pay any contractor, get a Form W-9. It gives you their legal name, business name, tax classification and taxpayer ID, either a Social Security number or an EIN. Store it securely, because it contains sensitive information. If someone won't give you a W-9, you may have to withhold backup tax from their payments, so it's much easier to collect it at the start, as part of onboarding.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a W-9 form with a lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paying
segments.narration: Pay contractors from your business account, against an invoice, and keep the invoice with the payment record. That's your proof of the business expense. Contractor payments go on Schedule C, line eleven, contract labor. If a contractor also bills you for materials or travel, that can go in the same line or the matching category; the key is having the invoice.
segments.on_screen_text: Pay against an invoice · Schedule C line 11
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice with a payment arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1099-NEC
segments.narration: In January, you may owe them a Form ten ninety-nine NEC. For payments made in twenty twenty-six, the threshold is two thousand dollars or more to one person for services in the year, and it's adjusted for inflation after that, so check the current figure. It's due to the contractor and to the IRS by January thirty-first. You can file it online through the IRS's free filing system for information returns. Payments to corporations are generally excluded, with some exceptions like attorneys.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a January calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Card payments
segments.narration: There's one big exception that saves paperwork. If you paid a contractor by credit card, or through a payment network like PayPal goods and services, you don't file a ten ninety-nine NEC for those payments. The payment company reports them instead, on a ten ninety-nine K. If you paid by bank transfer, check or Zelle, the ten ninety-nine NEC is yours to file. Keep a note of how you paid each person.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a card and a phone. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three questions
segments.narration: Before you pay anyone for help, there are three questions worth asking yourself. First, am I buying a result or renting someone's time? A result points to a contractor; time on my schedule points to an employee. Second, do they have their own business, with other clients and their own tools? Third, how will I pay them, and have I collected their W-9 first? If you can answer all three clearly, you've done most of the work of getting this right.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding up three fingers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your kids
segments.narration: Now family. If you're a sole proprietor, or a partnership owned only by you and your spouse, and you pay your own child for real work, the rules are unusually favorable. Wages paid to your child under eighteen aren't subject to Social Security and Medicare tax. Under twenty-one, they're not subject to federal unemployment tax. The wages are a deductible business expense for you, and your child can earn up to their standard deduction with no federal income tax, if they have no other income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small desk with a lamp. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Kid rules
segments.narration: But it has to be done properly. The work must be real and needed by your business: filing, data entry, packing orders, social media, cleaning the office. The pay has to be reasonable for that work, what you'd pay anyone else. Keep timesheets with dates, hours and tasks. Pay from the business account. And because it's employment, you run payroll and issue a W-2, not a ten ninety-nine. A seven-year-old earning fifty dollars an hour for social media won't hold up.
segments.on_screen_text: Real work, fair pay, timesheets, W-2
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a timesheet and a W-2. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Spouse
segments.narration: Paying your spouse is different. A spouse who works as your employee is subject to Social Security and Medicare tax, so there's no payroll-tax saving, though the wages are still a business expense. It can make sense for other reasons, like building their own Social Security record or giving them access to a retirement plan. If you and your spouse both own the business, that's a separate set of rules about partnerships and qualified joint ventures.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two rings and a pay stub. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Costs deductible
segments.narration: Whatever route you choose, the cost of help is a business expense: contractor invoices, employee wages, the employer share of payroll taxes, and payroll software fees. Hiring help often pays for itself if it frees up billable hours. If an assistant costs twenty-five dollars an hour and frees an hour you bill at seventy-five, the business is fifty dollars better off before tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin moving from one jar to another. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Overseas
segments.narration: Hiring a contractor who lives outside the US and works only from abroad? You generally don't file a ten ninety-nine for them. Instead, collect a Form W-8BEN, which confirms they're a foreign person. Keep it with your records alongside the invoices.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a globe and a form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Contractor or employee depends on control, money and the relationship, not on the label. Get a W-9 before the first payment, pay against invoices, and file ten ninety-nine NECs by January thirty-first for two thousand dollars or more, unless you paid by card or PayPal goods and services. Paying your child under eighteen in a sole proprietorship avoids Social Security and Medicare tax, if the work is real and documented. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes shaking hands with a helper. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Getting paid on time: freelance contracts, deposits and late fees
script.hook: Late payments are one of the most stressful parts of freelancing, and they're also one of the most preventable. Most of the fix happens before the work starts, in a few lines of a contract and a couple of habits around invoicing. In this video we'll take apart four myths that keep freelancers waiting for money, look at a cash-flow chart that shows why payment terms matter as much as your rate, and then go step by step from deposit to late fee to what to do when a client simply doesn't pay. Education, not legal or tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Late payments are one of the most stressful parts of freelancing, and they're also one of the most preventable. Most of the fix happens before the work starts, in a few lines of a contract and a couple of habits around invoicing. In this video we'll take apart four myths that keep freelancers waiting for money, look at a cash-flow chart that shows why payment terms matter as much as your rate, and then go step by step from deposit to late fee to what to do when a client simply doesn't pay. Education, not legal or tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding an invoice and a clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 1
segments.narration: Myth one: net thirty is just how business works. Fact: net thirty is a request, not a law. Big companies often have payment cycles you can't change, but plenty of clients will agree to shorter terms, or to a deposit, if you ask before the work starts. Net thirty after delivery means you do all the work and then lend the client your money for a month. You're allowed to propose something else.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a split card, myth and fact. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 2
segments.narration: Myth two: asking for a deposit scares good clients away. Fact: deposits are normal for project work, and clients who hire freelancers regularly expect them. Fifty percent upfront is common. A deposit also tells you something useful early. A client who won't pay anything before work starts may not pay everything after it's done. That's not always true, but it's worth noticing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin going in first. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 3
segments.narration: Myth three: late fees are rude. Fact: a late fee that's in the contract isn't a punishment, it's a term both of you agreed to. Most of the time you won't even charge it. Its job is to move your invoice up the pile, because a payables team pays the invoice that costs money to delay before the one that doesn't. Check your state's rules on how much you can charge.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small clock with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myth 4
segments.narration: Myth four: contracts are only for big projects. Fact: a one-page agreement is enough for small work, and it's the small clients without a procurement department where things go wrong most often. One page that says what you'll deliver, when, for how much, when it's due, and what happens if it's late, prevents most arguments before they start.

segments.heading: Cash flow
segments.narration: Here's why terms matter as much as your rate. Picture an eight-thousand-dollar project that takes six weeks. On net thirty after delivery, you invoice in week six and get paid around week ten, if they're on time. For ten weeks, your bank balance only goes down. With a fifty percent deposit, four thousand arrives in week one and four thousand around week eight. Same price, same work, but the deposit version has cash in the bank from the start. On a retainer paid in advance, you're paid before the month begins.

segments.heading: Deposit how
segments.narration: How to ask for a deposit: put it in the proposal, not as a surprise later. Fifty percent to book the start date, fifty percent on delivery. For longer projects, split it into milestones, like thirty, forty, thirty. Send the deposit invoice with the contract, and don't start until it's paid. That last part matters: if you start before the deposit arrives, it's just a promise.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a contract and an invoice together. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Invoicing day
segments.narration: Invoice the day you deliver. Not at the end of the month, not when you get around to it. Every day you wait is a day added to the payment clock. If you do ongoing work, invoice on the same date every month. Put a payment link right on the invoice, so paying takes one click. The easier you make it, the sooner it happens.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with today circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Due dates
segments.narration: Write the due date as a date. Due June thirtieth, twenty twenty-seven is harder to lose track of than net thirty, which someone has to count from a date they may not know. Include your payment terms, your late fee, an invoice number, the client's purchase order number if they use one, and what the invoice is for, in words the person approving it will understand.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a circled date. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who pays
segments.narration: Ask on day one who actually pays invoices. The person you work with is often not the person who processes payments. Some companies need you set up as a vendor first, with a W-9 and banking details, which can take weeks. Doing that during onboarding, not after the first invoice, can save you a month.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two people, one with a stamp. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Reminders
segments.narration: When an invoice is late, follow up on a schedule. One day overdue: a friendly reminder with the invoice and payment link. Seven days: ask for the date it will be paid, and offer to contact whoever processes it. Twenty-one days: refer to the contract, mention the late fee and that new work will pause until it's settled. Each message is short, polite and asks for one specific thing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three envelopes in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Late fees
segments.narration: When you do apply a late fee, apply it the way the contract says, from the date it says, and show it as a separate line on a new invoice. Many freelancers offer to waive it if the invoice is paid within a week. That's fine; the fee did its job if the money arrives. What doesn't work is threatening a fee that isn't in the contract.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice with an extra line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pausing work
segments.narration: The most powerful line in a freelance contract is often the right to pause work when an invoice is overdue. Continuing to work for a client who isn't paying increases what you're owed and reduces your leverage. Pausing politely, with notice, almost always gets a faster response than another reminder.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pause symbol. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Kill fee
segments.narration: Add a kill fee for projects that end early. If the client cancels midway, they pay for the work done so far, plus a set percentage for the time you reserved. It protects you from holding six weeks open and then having nothing to bill. Pair it with a notice period for retainers, such as thirty days.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a door with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Small claims
segments.narration: If a client simply won't pay, you have options. A final demand letter that sets a deadline often works. After that, small claims court handles disputes up to a limit set by each state, without needing a lawyer. Collections agencies take a percentage. For larger amounts, talk to a lawyer. Which route makes sense depends on how much is owed and how much time you're willing to spend.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a gavel next to an envelope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes on unpaid
segments.narration: One tax note. If you use the cash method, as most freelancers do, you don't pay tax on an invoice until you're paid. So an unpaid invoice doesn't cost you tax, but it also isn't a deduction if it's never paid, because it was never counted as income. Expenses you paid for that project are still deductible. That's why prevention, not a write-off, is the real protection.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin that stays out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retainers
segments.narration: For ongoing work, a retainer is the strongest payment term of all. The client pays a fixed amount at the start of each month for a set amount of your time or a set list of deliverables. You know what's coming in, the client knows what they're getting, and nobody chases anyone. Spell out what happens to unused hours, whether they roll over or expire, and how much notice either side gives to end it.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Keep a simple payments log: client, invoice number, amount, date sent, date due, date paid. Once a month, look at the average number of days each client takes to pay. That number tells you which clients to ask for deposits, and which terms to tighten when you renew.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a table with three columns. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Net thirty is negotiable, deposits are normal, late fees in a contract are fair, and even small jobs need a one-page agreement. Ask for a deposit with the contract and don't start until it's paid. Invoice the day you deliver, with a real due date and a payment link. Find out who pays. Follow up on day one, seven and twenty-one, and use the right to pause. The Rate and Contract Kit in the description has templates for all of this. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
